title: The long-game drill: How investing may fit into your financial plan.
summary: Learn how investing may fit into a broader financial plan and how managed portfolios can provide a more hands-off investing experience.
body_markdown:
Long-term goals tend to look like:


-


Retirement


-


Long-term wealth building


-


Education planning


-


A future lifestyle goal


-


Financial independence


What these have in common is distance. They sit far enough out that money set aside for them is not money you expect to touch soon. No single product is appropriate for every goal, and the right approach depends on the goal itself.


The Securities and Exchange Commission describes your time horizon as the number of months, years, or decades you plan to invest to reach a goal, and notes that investors with a longer time horizon may feel comfortable taking on riskier or more volatile investments, while those with a shorter horizon may prefer less volatile ones. ([Asset allocation, Investor.gov](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/getting-started/asset-allocation) )


The word doing the work there is “may.” A longer horizon can give an investment more time to recover from a decline. It does not remove the possibility of the decline, guarantee a recovery, or make any outcome certain.


The SEC defines risk tolerance as your ability and willingness to lose some or all of your original investment in exchange for potentially greater returns. Two words there, and they are not the same test:


-


Ability is structural—whether a loss would actually damage your finances


-


Willingness is emotional—whether you could watch a decline without abandoning the plan


Someone can have high ability and low willingness, or the reverse. The honest question is not how you feel about risk in the abstract. It is what you would actually do if you opened the app and the balance was meaningfully lower than what you put in.


If the honest answer is that you would sell, that is worth knowing before you begin, not during.


They serve different jobs:


-


Savings is often used for accessible cash and nearer-term goals; investing is often considered for longer-term goals


-


Savings generally earns interest; investment values can rise or fall


-


Deposit accounts may be FDIC insured within applicable limits; securities are not FDIC insured


-


Savings may offer greater liquidity; investing may carry market and investment risk


Neither one is the better tool. They are different tools, and using one for the other's job is where most trouble starts.


Broadly, there are three routes: self-directed investing, where you choose and manage everything yourself; professionally managed portfolios, where allocation and ongoing management are handled for you; and some combination of the two.


This is a preference question, not a sophistication question. Plenty of financially capable people choose managed portfolios because they would rather spend their attention elsewhere, and that is a legitimate reason.


The typical process:


-


Answer questions about your goals, preferences, and financial stage


-


Consider an asset allocation appropriate to those answers


-


Choose a manager and model, where applicable


-


Monitor the portfolio digitally


-


Review and adjust as your circumstances change


We publish investing insights and a set of free calculators, including an APY calculator for comparing what a deposit account would earn over the same period, on its[planning hub](https://www.axosbank.com/personal/plan) .


Comparing the two side by side is a reasonable exercise before deciding which job a given dollar should do.


Here is the part most introductory investing content skips, and it is the single most useful thing to understand at the start: fees are the only number in investing you can know in advance. Returns are uncertain. Costs are not.


Managed investing typically involves a few layers—a management or model fee charged as a percentage of your assets, the expense ratios of the underlying funds, and in some cases a minimum annual account fee. That last one deserves particular attention if you are starting small, because a flat minimum behaves very differently on a small balance than a percentage does.


The move: convert every fee into a dollar figure against the balance you plan to hold, not against a hypothetical larger one. A fee expressed as a fraction of a percent sounds negligible. A flat annual minimum on a starter balance may not be. Neither is wrong, but you should know which one applies to you before you open the account, and any provider worth using will tell you plainly.
